# The Present Status of Certificate Verification (Ground Truth)

In my community (Tamale) and the country at large, certificate verification has been a major challenge and the reason been that, the traditional methods involve time-consuming processes such as contacting issuing institutions to confirm authenticity, which is often inefficient given the vast number of graduates. Such manual verification systems are highly susceptible to fraud, as falsified or replicated certificates can be created through tampering, compromising the integrity of academic and professional credentials

The present state of verification of certificate is:

Ø  Manual verification (contacting universities)

Ø  Centralized database (GTEC)

There is no platform which or domain which can give instance verification of certificate as when is needed in real time.

The resultant of lack of real time verification is that;

Ø  High fraud and forgery rates

Ø  Slow cross-border authentication

Affected people of this slow or prolong delay;

Ø  Students waiting for admission

Ø  Job seekers

Ø  Security agency

Ø  NGO’s

Lack of real time verification brings down the moral and slow down the process of admitting students into universities and employment.

Insights (What we learned)

The analysis reveals that centralized certificate systems are inherently vulnerable due to their reliance on single administrative authorities. Shifting trust from institutions to cryptographic mechanisms enhances system robustness and transparency. Separating certificate storage from verification functions improves scalability and performance, making the system more adaptable to growing credential volumes.

What is consistent everywhere?

Every institution does their own certificate verification

What surprise us is?

The verification process of each university varies from the other. While some do the verification through the Academic Directorate others does it through heads of department and then through quality assurance.

The core insight

The challenge here is that, the institutions are not intentionally delaying the process of certificate verification but rather they are dealing with large data request at almost every time.  There should be a trusted platform or website to link these universities to the numerous requests for certificate verification. The idea of a trusted platform is not to replace the on-going approach of certificate verification by the universities but rather provide a secure platform to help lessen the work load.

HYPOTHESES (what we trust can work)

Ø  If certificates are hashed and stored on IPFS, integrity can be guaranteed

Ø  If hashes are anchored on blockchain, verification becomes trustless

Ø  Smart contracts can automate certificate issuance and revocation

Our central hypothesis

Blockchain and IPFS introduce a decentralized approach to certificate verification that fundamentally transforms trust models in credential management. By anchoring certificate hashes on a blockchain and storing the actual certificate data on IPFS, the system ensures immutability, transparency, and global accessibility. Verification becomes instant and trustless, eliminating the need for intermediaries or direct contact with issuing institutions.

IPFS solution (What we developing)

One of the most notable aspects of blockchain-based verification is the ability to verify certificates without exposing sensitive personal data. Public verification mechanisms confirm authenticity while preserving privacy. Additionally, certificates remain accessible regardless of the issuing institution’s operational status, increasing system resilience. This level of openness and permanence represents a paradigm shift in how credentials are managed and trusted

How it works

1.       Content Addressing (Core Idea)

Ø  Every file is hashed using cryptography (SHA-256)

Ø  The hash becomes a CID (content Identifier)

Ø  If the content chances, the CID changes

Ø  This guarantees data integrity and immutability

2.       File Chunking

When a file is added to IPFS:

Ø  Large files are split into small chunks

Ø  Each chunk is hashed separately

Ø  Hashes are organized into Merkle Directed Acyclic Graph

3.       Distributed Hash Table (DHT)

IPFS uses a DHT to locate content

Ø  Nodes announce: “I have CID X”

Ø  The DHT maps CID

Ø  No central server

4.       Peer to Peer Retrieval

When user request a file;

Ø  You ask the network for the CID

Ø  DHT finds peers storing that CID

Ø  Data is downloaded from Multiple peers simultaneously

Ø  Chunks are reassembled locally

5.       Local Caching

Ø  Once user download content, user node can serve it

Ø  Popular content spreads naturally

Ø  Reduces network load and latency

6.       Pinning

by default, IPFS does not guarantee permanent storage.

To keep data available

Ø  Pin the content on a node

Ø  Or use pinning services (IPFS cluster, filecoin)

7.       IPNS (optional mutable data)

Since CIDs are immutable:

Ø  IPNS allows updatable pointers

Ø  Maps a stable name

Ø  Useful for websites and dynamic content

8.       Security Features

Ø  Integrity: Hash verification ensures data is unaltered

Ø  Tamper proof: any modification changes the CID

Ø  No single point of failure

The Opportunities of IPFS brings

Ø  Blockchain-based certificate verification paves the way for self-sovereign digital credentials, empowering individuals to autonomously control and manage their academic and professional qualifications.

Ø  Interoperability across institutions facilitates frictionless recognition of credentials across international boundaries and diverse sectors.

Ø  Contemporary developments, including remote recruitment, virtual learning platforms, and national digital credential programs, reinforce the imperative for adoption.

Ø  Joint efforts by universities, industry partners, and accrediting entities are crucial to devising governance protocols and fostering broad endorsement of decentralized credential infrastructures.

The Community Impact

Ø  Decentralized access to information

Ø  Reduce costs for content sharing

Ø  Improve data availability and reliability

Ø  Secure storage of public and community records

Opportunities in the long term:

Final Summary

Ø  Ground Truth: Rising cases of fake academic and professional certificates

Ø  Insights: Centralized certificate systems are a single point of failure

Ø  Hypotheses: If certificates are hashed and stored on IPFS, integrity can be guaranteed

Ø  Opportunities: Verification without intermediaries
